title: Everyday Laws Every Person Should Know
summary: Ten legal principles and golden rules that keep you safe in ordinary life.

body.text: You do not need to be a lawyer to stay out of trouble. A handful of legal principles cover most of what happens in ordinary life.

items: Constitution: every person has Fundamental Rights - equality before the law, freedom of speech, and protection of life and personal liberty. Courts can strike down government action that violates them.

Criminal law: an offence is a wrong punishable by law; a complaint is your written information to the police; an FIR is the formal first record of a cognisable offence; an arrest is custody; a court case decides guilt. Knowing which is which prevents panic.
Evidence: what you keep decides what you can prove. Preserve messages, emails, receipts, photos and CCTV details, and collect them lawfully.
Public behaviour: excessive noise, public nuisance, trespassing, assault and damaging property can all attract penalties, even when they feel minor.
Privacy: guard your Aadhaar, PAN, bank details and personal photos. Careless sharing can lead to fraud or blackmail.
Women's safety: the law protects against stalking, harassment, domestic violence and workplace sexual harassment.
Child protection: child labour is restricted, and children have special protection against sexual offences under the POCSO Act.
Taxes: know your income tax basics - Form 16, AIS, TDS, and when you must file a return.
Agreements: before signing, read the payment terms, penalties and termination clauses. What you sign binds you.
Civic duties: follow waste-disposal rules, protect public property and obey local regulations. These are legal duties, not just etiquette.
Never sign a document you have not read or understood.
Never share an OTP, UPI PIN or banking password with anyone.
Keep copies of employment contracts, loan agreements, receipts and important correspondence.
If police or another authority contacts you, stay calm, cooperate lawfully, and ask for clarification if you do not understand the procedure.
If someone threatens you, do not escalate the situation; preserve evidence and seek appropriate help.
Never ignore a court summons, legal notice or official deadline without understanding its consequences.
Verify legal claims on official government websites instead of trusting viral social-media videos.
For a serious legal problem, get advice from a qualified lawyer rather than relying only on general online information.

body.text: Not every right is absolute. Many rights carry reasonable restrictions, and the exact rule can depend on your state and the facts of your case.
When in doubt, keep the paper and ask for it in writing. A written record is far stronger than a memory.

practicalSteps: Save 112, 1930, 1915 and 15100 in your phone today.
Keep a folder (physical or on cloud) of your key documents and receipts.
Before signing anything, ask for a copy and time to read it.
Note dates, names and reference numbers whenever something happens.
exceptions: Fundamental Rights apply mainly against the State, though a few also apply to private persons.
A declared emergency can restrict some rights, but Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

faqs.q: Does ignorance of the law excuse me?
faqs.a: Generally no. Ignorance is rarely a defence, which is exactly why these basics matter.

faqs.q: How do I check whether a legal claim is true?
faqs.a: Use official sources - India Code, the department website and the specific Act - not forwarded messages or short videos.

misconceptions.fact: Most rights carry reasonable restrictions, and their exact scope depends on the law and the facts.
